topic: TCP connection establishment and the three-way handshake

  The "three-way handshake" is the procedure used to establish a
  connection.  This procedure normally is initiated by one TCP and
  responded to by another TCP.  The procedure also works if two TCP
  simultaneously initiate the procedure.  When simultaneous attempt
  occurs, each TCP receives a "SYN" segment which carries no
  acknowledgment after it has sent a "SYN".  Of course, the arrival of
  an old duplicate "SYN" segment can potentially make it appear, to the
  recipient, that a simultaneous connection initiation is in progress.
  Proper use of "reset" segments can disambiguate these cases.

  The principle reason for the three-way handshake is to prevent old
  duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion.  To deal with
  this, a special control message, reset, has been devised.  If the
  receiving TCP is in a  non-synchronized state (i.e., SYN-SENT,
  SYN-RECEIVED), it returns to LISTEN on receiving an acceptable reset.

kept.question: What is the purpose of the three‑way handshake in TCP?
kept.answer: It is the procedure used to establish a connection between two TCPs.

kept.question: Which segments are exchanged during the three‑way handshake?
kept.answer: A SYN segment, a SYN‑ACK segment, and an ACK segment.

kept.question: What state does a TCP enter after receiving a SYN‑ACK segment?
What mechanism does TCP use to prevent old duplicate SYN segments from causing confusion?
Why must data be buffered until the connection reaches the ESTABLISHED state?
kept.answer: Because data‑carrying segments may be part of the connection initiation and should not be delivered until the connection is established.
